title: Client flags and proxy solutions brief (field vignettes)
body:
Purpose: quick synthesis of recent customer flags (Apr–May 2026) with lightweight, low-risk proxy solutions we can trial fast. This is intentionally pragmatic — we want deployable band-aids and experiments to buy time before larger product work.

Context: over the last 6 weeks CS + Solutions teams logged ~48 tickets that cluster into three recurring friction patterns. Many customers are enterprise platform teams or AI-native startups trying to stabilize inference cost or reliability during peak loads. Notes below are field-sourced, unfiltered, and include direct quotes where helpful.

Summary of recurring themes (rough frequency buckets):
- Latency variability during burst windows (high frequency, ~21/48 tickets).
- Unexpected output regression after model rollouts / quantization switches (medium frequency, ~12/48).
- Confusion about routing & fallback behavior across Dedicated vs Hosted (low-medium, ~9/48).
- Billing/observability gaps for cached vs live tokens (sporadic, ~6/48).

Vignettes (raw, abbreviated):
1) Vignette: Retail search company (large PLG account) — "Search spikes around promo windows — latency doubles for 30m, autoscaling feels slow, and our SLAs blow up. We see many 504s and fallback to smaller models which are garbage." Notes: customer uses Dedicated + burst; cares about deterministic tail latency.
2) Vignette: Fintech analytics startup — "After switching to int8 quantized variant our summarization accuracy dipped for named entities. Can we pin model version per route?" Notes: emphasizes quality regressions and opaque rollout effects.
3) Vignette: Healthcare partner (on Private) — "We're unsure how routing rules work when a region is unhealthy — will traffic go to Hosted? We can't risk PHI leaving our VPC." Notes: concerns about automatic region fallback & data egress.

Observed signal patterns + quick interpretation:
- Latency bursts typically correlate with small cohorts that send large synchronous requests (batch-y workloads) rather than steady QPS. Many customers have long-tail inter-arrival distributions.
- Regression reports often follow automatic rollouts where an optimized quantized variant replaced a float baseline; customers equate 'optimized' with 'less accurate' because they lack per-prompt evals.
- Routing confusion stems from two things: terminology mismatch in UI/SDK ("fallback") and lack of a visible audit trail for where traffic went during an incident.

Proxy solutions we can trial in 2–4 weeks (low dev cost):
A) Burst-guard routing (config toggle): ephemeral per-customer short-circuit that, under detected tail latency, redirects to a warm pool of pre-warmed instances running the float baseline (or a known-good variant) for a bounded window (e.g., 10m). Implementation: policy + react hook; minimal infra change if we reuse existing warm pool primitives. Expected impact: reduces 504s and SLA violations for bursty events. Risks: cost during activation; false positives if detection too sensitive.
B) Quantization-impact quick-eval: small CLI tool or SDK hook customers can run that compares a tiny holdout prompt set of 30 examples across baseline vs optimized variant and emits a compact delta report (tokens to watch: entities, dates, numeric precision). Implementation: library + template prompt set. Expected impact: reduce surprise regressions and make rollouts more transparent. Risks: customers won't run it unless we integrate into rollout pipeline or offer an incentive.
C) Routing visibility tape: sticky log + UI panel that shows per-minute routing decisions during incidents and the active policy that triggered them. Implementation: expose existing trace logs in aggregated form. Expected impact: reduces confusion and reduces CS back-and-forth. Risks: extra retention/cost; UI work required.
D) Billing attribution label: tag cached vs compute tokens and export to billing CSV with a flag; small addition but helps commercial conversations. Implementation: add a metadata flag to existing usage pipeline. Expected impact: reduces invoice disputes. Risks: minimal.

Prioritization (quick):
- P0: Burst-guard routing (A) — top pain for high-paying customers; mitigates SLA violations.
- P1: Quantization-impact quick-eval (B) — prevents recurring quality tickets; relatively low implementation cost.
- P2: Routing visibility tape (C) — high customer confidence value but larger UX work.
- P3: Billing attribution label (D) — small ops lift; negotiate with finance for rollout.

Proposed owners & rough ETA:
- Burst-guard routing: eng-serving-runtime (owner: Jun Park) + SRE; prototype 2 weeks, limited pilot 4–6 weeks.
- Quick-eval tool: applied-ml + developer-experience (owner: Maya Ortiz); MVP 1–2 weeks (script), integrate in rollout pipeline 4–6 weeks.
- Routing visibility: observability team (owner: Liam O'Connor); wireframe 1 week, dev 4–8 weeks.
- Billing attribution: finance + platform-engineering; spec 1 week, deploy 2–3 weeks.

Suggested pilot plan (first two weeks):
1) Select 3 customer partners (one retail, one fintech, one healthcare) willing to pilot burst-guard routing in a limited roll (safety net + opt-in).
2) Ship a CLI quick-eval and ask pilot customers to run pre-rollout. Collect 30 example prompts and the delta report.
3) Run a post-pilot sync after 3 weeks to capture signal and decide next steps.

Measurement & success criteria:
- For Burst-guard routing: reduce 95th–99th tail latency during bursts by 30% and reduce incident reopen rate by 50% for pilot customers.
- For Quick-eval: decrease 'regression' tickets after rollouts by 60% for customers that used the tool.
- For Routing visibility: CS response time to routing inquiries drops from avg 3 days to <24h.

Tradeoffs and risks:
- Cost vs reliability: burst-guard increases short-term cost for reliability; need executive alignment on when to absorb vs pass-on.
- False confidence: quick-eval is not exhaustive; customers may assume safety from a small test set. Need careful messaging.
- Data residency: any automated fallback that moves traffic off-customer VPC must be explicitly opt-in for regulated accounts.

Open questions to resolve in next sync:
- Can we reuse existing pre-warmed pools or need a new class for burst-guard? (infra)
- Who signs off on cost-absorbing policies for short guard windows? (finance/ops)
- What is the minimal prompt set that gives statistically useful signals for quantization impact? (applied-ml)
- UX: how transparent should toggles be vs managed options for enterprise? (product + legal)

Action items (short):
- [Aisha] Schedule 30‑min scoping with Jun + Liam + Maya (by 2026-05-13).
- [Jun] Inventory warm pool capacity & ability to tag by variant (by 2026-05-14).
- [Maya] Draft quick-eval CLI and sample prompt set template (by 2026-05-15).
- [Liam] Prototype routing visibility wireframe and note log retention needs (by 2026-05-18).
- [CS] Recruit 3 pilot customers and get NDAs/opt-in approvals (by 2026-05-20).

Notes to self / negotiation points for PMs:
- Keep language conservative: frame burst-guard as an operational safety valve, not as a replacement for proper autoscaling fixes.
- Consider a chargeback model for prolonged guard activation to avoid cost surprises.
- This doc should be iterated after pilot; capture real numbers and anonymized customer quotes for exec summary.

Raw customer quotes (anonymized):
- "During promo hours it's chaos — our search SLA just evaporates." — Retail partner
- "We lost two named entities in a report after a quant rollout; it changed the meaning." — Fintech
- "We can't have any traffic leave the VPC; fallback must stay internal." — Healthcare partner

End of brief.

-- Aisha (CS): feedback welcome; drop notes inline or ping #cs-field-labs.
